item.description: Tropical Storm Bertha’s landfall, the House vote on a $95 billion Iran-war budget package, a sharp drop in homicide rates across major U.S. cities, and a new legal fight over Pentagon testosterone policy lead the national brief before Debt Desk turns to Wednesday’s verified Treasury curve, the latest official SOFR print, fresh CRE and multifamily financings across banks, life company capital and private credit, CMBS refinance friction, agency updates, and one thing to watch for Thursday, Jul
item.content:encoded:
It is Thursday, July 23rd, and this is Debt Desk.

National

Let’s start with the national morning brief, because the macro setup today is a mix of live weather risk, wartime fiscal politics, a surprisingly constructive public-safety datapoint, and another legal fight that says a lot about how Washington is governing right now.

The first story this morning is Tropical Storm Bertha, and this is a clear continuity story from earlier in the week with a real new development overnight. The storm made landfall in St. Bernard Parish, Louisiana, about 40 miles east of New Orleans, early Thursday and kept moving west toward Texas with sustained winds around 45 miles an hour. That matters less because of headline wind speed and more because it keeps the Gulf operating map unsettled. Warnings stretched from Alabama to Louisiana, parts of the coast were closed, and forecasters were still looking for one to four inches of rain with locally higher amounts. For lenders, owners and operators, this is the kind of storm that can be modest in category but still disruptive in practice. It can slow inspections, complicate insurance conversations, delay crews, and keep property-level cash planning a little tighter along the coast.

The second story is in Washington, where the House adopted a $95 billion Republican-backed budget package tied to the Iran war and other Trump priorities. That vote matters because it keeps the conflict from being only a foreign-policy headline. It pulls the war more directly into the domestic fiscal conversation and keeps energy, inflation and shipping risk close to the business day. Senate skepticism is still part of the story, so this is not a settled funding path yet. But the signal from the House is that the administration still has meaningful support for sustaining the current posture even as the political and market costs rise.

The third story is one of the more encouraging datapoints we have seen in a while. The Associated Press reported this morning that a new Council on Criminal Justice report showed an 18 percent decline in homicide rates across 30 American cities compared with the same period a year ago, which works out to about 215 fewer homicides. If that pace holds, the annual homicide rate could fall to the lowest level in more than a century once the final numbers are in. That does not mean every city is improving at the same speed, and the report also showed small increases in shoplifting, domestic violence, sexual assaults and drug offenses. But the broader read is still useful. A calmer crime backdrop does not solve every urban operating problem, yet it does matter for retail traffic, leasing sentiment, municipal confidence and the general narrative around city recovery.

The fourth story is a more targeted legal fight, but it is worth carrying because it speaks to the administration’s governing style. A federal judge questioned the difference between the Pentagon’s new testosterone screening and treatment initiative for service members and the military’s restrictions on transgender care. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s program would screen service members 30 and older each year and make treatment optional for younger personnel. The judge’s pushback tells you this issue is not staying inside a medical lane. It is becoming another constitutional and administrative-law test case around how the government draws distinctions between favored and disfavored classes of treatment.

So the national backdrop this morning is fairly sharp. Bertha is still a live operational story as it tracks west along the Gulf. The House has deepened the domestic political commitment to the Iran fight. Violent crime data are offering a more constructive signal on urban stability than many expected. And the Pentagon is getting judicial scrutiny over how it is drawing policy lines in the culture-war space. That is the setup for the debt conversation today.

Debt Desk

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor is rates, and these are the verified figures from the local checker using the official Treasury page and the New York Fed API. Because today is Thursday, July 23, and the Treasury market has not closed yet, the latest verified Treasury close available at run time is Wednesday, July 22. That curve closed at 4.31 percent on the 2-year, 4.41 percent on the 5-year, 4.67 percent on the 10-year, and 5.15 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.62 percent for July 22.

That curve is still telling the same broad story, but with a little more pressure at the long end than borrowers would like. The front end is elevated, yet the bigger problem for many commercial borrowers is still duration. A 2-year at 4.31 and a 5-year at 4.41 are not easy numbers, but they are workable if the business plan is short, the asset is improving and the sponsor has conviction around execution speed. A 10-year at 4.67 and a 30-year at 5.15 keep permanent debt expensive and make longer fixed-rate certainty feel more like a premium product. In plain English, capital is available, but term still costs real money.

That helps explain why the freshest deal flow keeps splitting by asset quality, sponsorship and loan purpose instead of moving as one clean reopening story.

On the private-credit side, Commercial Observer reported Wednesday afternoon that CDK Lending provided $36.7 million of pre-development financing for RBH Group’s planned 420-unit mixed-use apartment project at 101 Market Street in Newark. The debt pays off a previous Goldman Sachs loan on the site. That is a useful signal because it is not stabilized cash flow debt and it is not a trophy headline. It is pre-development money for a large urban apartment project, which tells you there is still lender appetite for housing growth stories when the location, assemblage and path forward are credible enough.

We also have another reminder that residential construction debt is still clearing when the sponsorship and market are obvious. Commercial Observer reported this week that Witkoff and Monroe Capital secured a $302.6 million construction loan from Athene and J.P. Morgan for the first phase of 700 North Miami Avenue in Downtown Miami. The first phase is planned for about 890 units. That lender mix matters. You have bank capital and insurance capital working together on a large, visible multifamily story in a market lenders still know well. That is not a sign of indiscriminate risk appetite, but it is a sign that the better apartment development stories can still pull real size.

Banks are still active farther down the size curve too. Commercial Observer reported that M&T provided roughly $25.5 million of acquisition financing for Hope’s Crossing, a 125-unit apartment property in Toms River, New Jersey. Again, that is not a flashy headline, but it is important because it shows conventional apartment business is still executable with regional bank money when the basis, sponsorship and property story are straightforward.

Private credit remains a core release valve wherever speed, flexibility or asset complexity matter more than cheapest possible pricing. Commercial Observer reported this week that Affinius Capital and Axonic Capital provided a $42.5 million refinance for a two-property self-storage portfolio in Coral Gables and Pembroke Pines. It was the fifth joint origination between those firms, and the lenders pointed to supply-constrained submarkets and sustained population growth. That is a clean reminder that debt funds are still very comfortable leaning into niches where traditional balance-sheet lenders may not spend the time.

There is also continued support for transitional office and mixed-use assets, but only when the collateral story is unusually clean. Commercial Observer reported that Hudson Bay Capital provided a $60 million bridge refinance for the redeveloped Bell Works Fort Monmouth campus in Tinton Falls, New Jersey, a 276,900-square-foot property that will become Jersey Mike’s headquarters. That is the office read-through today. Bridge lenders are still willing to back repurposed office or mixed-use product, but only when there is a visible tenant anchor, a reuse story the market can understand, and a sponsor who has already done enough work to make the underwrite believable.

Put those transactions together and the tone is fairly clear. Banks are lending into apartment acquisitions and construction where leverage and sponsorship make sense. Life company capital is still participating, but mostly in larger, higher-clarity residential deals. Debt funds and other private lenders continue to handle the messy middle, including pre-development, transitional assets and niche collateral. Nobody is acting as though credit is wide open. But nobody is acting as though the market is shut either.

That brings us to spreads and securitized execution. We do not have a fresh same-day conduit pricing headline to carry, so the cleaner market read comes from Trepp’s latest data and maturity work. Trepp said the overall CMBS delinquency rate fell 20 basis points in June to 7.35 percent. That looks better at the headline level, but the same June report still showed $2.64 billion of newly delinquent loans, with the five largest accounting for just under $1 billion of that total. Trepp’s July maturity work also says $76.6 billion of CMBS hard maturities are due in 2026, with 39 percent falling in the fourth quarter, and roughly 36 percent of those loans carrying debt yields at or below 8 percent. Office, retail and multifamily have the highest concentrations of that exposure.

The practical takeaway is that CMBS remains open for the right story, but refinance friction has not disappeared. It has just become more selective. Clean cash flow, cleaner leverage and assets that can survive secondary-market scrutiny still have a lane. Weak debt yield and uncertain exits still do not.

On the benchmark side, SOFR at 3.62 percent is not itself a dramatic move, but the combination of a relatively stable overnight base rate with a still-heavy 10-year and 30-year keeps floating-rate bridge debt more competitive than long-duration fixed executions for many sponsors. If you think you can create value in two or three years, floating bridge debt still makes sense. If you need to lock out long-term certainty today, you are still paying up for it.

Multifamily remains the deepest lane, and the latest tape keeps reinforcing that. We already mentioned Newark, Toms River and Downtown Miami. There is also a second-order datapoint from Commercial Observer that multifamily loan balances at U.S. banks reached $6.14 trillion in the first quarter of 2026, with multifamily balances up 53 percent since 2019. That does not mean every lender wants more apartment exposure right now, but it does underline how central multifamily remains to bank real estate books even as underwriting has grown more selective.

Agency activity still matters because it gives the apartment market a steadier outlet than most other property types have. Freddie Mac’s investor pages continue to show regular multifamily certificates issuance windows, and the platform now pushes investors toward its multifamily securities pricing tools as well. The main point for borrowers is simple: the Freddie lane is still functioning, and investors still have reasons to stay engaged with the agency bid.

Fannie Mae’s newest official visible update is more directly operational. Guide Update 26-18, effective July 20, covers near-stabilized property submissions. That is not a dramatic policy overhaul, but it is a useful signal that Fannie is still actively tuning the edge cases that matter most in today’s market, especially for assets that are almost but not fully stabilized. In an environment where a lot of apartment stories are good but not perfect, that kind of guidance matters.

On HUD and FHA, there was no major fresh multifamily policy headline overnight, and that is worth saying plainly rather than pretending otherwise. The better read is that the lane remains quietly functional. HUD’s ORCF underwriting queue page was updated as of July 22, which is not a headline by itself but does tell you the FHA machinery is still moving. In this market, operational continuity from HUD can be almost as important as a new splashy bulletin, especially for affordable and workforce housing sponsors that need a dependable execution alternative.

The concise market snapshot this morning is this. The latest verified Treasury close is 4.31 percent on the 2-year, 4.41 percent on the 5-year, 4.67 percent on the 10-year, and 5.15 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.62 percent for July 22. Banks are still lending, but mostly where the story is straightforward. Life company capital is still showing up, but largely for bigger, cleaner residential transactions. Debt funds remain essential for pre-development, transitional and specialized collateral. CMBS is better than the distress headlines alone would imply, but it is still selective. Multifamily remains the strongest lane, and agencies continue to matter.

One thing to watch today is whether the long end backs off at all or stays pinned high. If the 10-year and especially the 30-year keep holding these levels while SOFR stays relatively stable, the market will keep favoring shorter-duration structures, bridge debt and transitional executions over long fixed-rate takeouts. If the long end softens even modestly, you could see more borrowers try to term out while they can.

The takeaway for Thursday, July 23, is straightforward. Nationally, the day opens with a landfalling Gulf storm, a House vote that ties war spending more directly to the domestic agenda, an encouraging decline in homicides across major cities, and another legal test of the administration’s governing posture. In Debt Desk, the message is that capital is there, but duration is still expensive and selectivity still rules. Multifamily remains the clearest path to execution, private credit is still doing a lot of the hard work, and the long end of the Treasury curve is still the number that can change the tone of the whole day.

It is Tuesday, July 21st, and this is Debt Desk.

National

Let’s start with the national morning brief, because the macro backdrop is opening with a little more weather risk, a little more food-safety uncertainty, and another reminder that legal and security stories are still landing right on top of the business day.

The biggest operating story this morning is still the Gulf. The weather risk that was hanging over the northern Gulf Coast on Monday has now become Tropical Storm Bertha, and the Associated Press reported early Tuesday, July 21, that the storm was moving toward the Florida Panhandle and Alabama with sustained winds around 50 miles an hour. Bertha is not just a coastal weather headline. It matters because it is arriving while Texas is still dealing with flood cleanup from last week and while the Gulf logistics map is already a little more fragile than usual. When a system like this slows down, even if it never becomes a major storm, it can still disrupt trucking, labor schedules, port-adjacent activity, property inspections and basic business continuity across a wide stretch of the coast. For anyone who touches real estate, insurance or local credit, the story is less about the storm category and more about whether the cleanup window keeps getting pushed back.

The second story is the produce-chain story, and it is still moving in the wrong direction. AP reported Tuesday that the Food and Drug Administration remains focused on Taylor Farms as the source of a cyclospora outbreak even after the agency backed away from a faulty positive test result. That is continuity from the weekend, but it is meaningful continuity. The lettuce recall already widened to products shipped to 27 states, and now the government is effectively saying the traceback case still holds even though one lab result did not. That keeps the story alive for restaurants, distributors and retailers because it tells operators the issue is not resolved by one corrected test. Once a recall starts to hit consumer trust, tenant sales and sourcing behavior, it becomes a broader operating story, not just a public-health bulletin.

The third story is the attack outside the federal building at 26 Federal Plaza in Manhattan. AP reported Tuesday that an ex-soldier started a fire and fired a pellet gun outside the building, injuring three people, including two government employees and one civilian who was there for an immigration hearing. The event does not look systemically important on its own, but it lands in a building that houses immigration and federal law-enforcement functions, and that makes it part of the wider national-security and immigration-enforcement atmosphere rather than an isolated local disturbance. It is another example of how political stress and operational risk are now sharing the same physical spaces in major cities.

The fourth story is the legal escalation tied to immigration enforcement. AP reported Monday, July 20, that the Justice Department activated the Alien Terrorist Removal Court for the first time since Congress created it in 1996, and the judge immediately asked the government for more information after the initial filing. That is worth carrying forward because it is not just a courtroom curiosity. It signals that the administration is still looking for harder, less-tested legal tools and is willing to move into channels that had been dormant for decades. Markets do not trade directly off that headline this morning, but labor-sensitive sectors, cross-border businesses and anyone underwriting political noise into a business plan should pay attention to the posture.

So the national setup for Tuesday is fairly clean. The Gulf is still exposed. The lettuce recall story is broader and more persistent than operators would like. A federal building attack in Manhattan sharpened the security mood around immigration-related facilities. And Washington is still experimenting with a tougher legal lane. That is the backdrop for the debt conversation today.

Debt Desk

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor is still rates, and the numbers in this script are the verified numbers from the local checker. Because the official Treasury table for Tuesday, July 21, is not posted yet, the latest verified Treasury close available at run time is Monday, July 20. That curve closed at 4.21 percent on the 2-year, 4.33 percent on the 5-year, 4.60 percent on the 10-year, and 5.11 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.59 percent for July 17, according to the New York Fed.

That curve is still doing two things at once. The front end is not friendly, but it is manageable enough to keep shorter fixed-rate executions and floating-rate structures in play. The long end is where the friction really shows up. A 30-year Treasury north of 5 percent keeps permanent debt expensive, stretches debt-service coverage, and makes long-duration certainty feel like a luxury product rather than the default answer. The gap between the 2-year and the 30-year is also a useful reminder that borrowers are still paying materially more for duration than for simply accessing capital. In plain English, money is available, but term is still expensive.

That helps explain the tone in the freshest deal tape. Commercial Observer reported on Monday afternoon that a PGIM, Tribeca Investment Group and Meadow Partners venture closed a $228.9 million refinancing for 295 Fifth Avenue in Midtown South. Rialto Capital Management, in partnership with Hines, supplied floating-rate, interest-only bridge debt for the newly renovated office tower. The property is only about 50 percent occupied, but it has enough leasing momentum and enough quality to attract a competitive refinancing process. That is the office lesson this morning. Lenders are not reopening the office lane in a broad, indiscriminate way. They are still backing office when the asset is newly improved, the location is liquid, and the path to stabilization looks tangible rather than theoretical.

We also got a cleaner read on where life company money is willing to meet bank money in residential construction. Commercial Observer reported Monday that Witkoff and Monroe Capital secured a $302.6 million construction loan for an 890-unit tower at 700 North Miami Avenue. Apollo’s Athene Annuity and Life Company and J.P. Morgan Chase provided the financing. That pairing matters. It suggests the better residential development stories can still pull together big-ticket capital stacks that blend bank balance-sheet credibility with insurance capital appetite, especially in a market like Downtown Miami where scale, location and sponsor visibility are all easy to underwrite. It also tells you life company capital is still active, but mostly where the collateral story is unusually clear.

Banks are still showing up on smaller and more conventional multifamily executions too. Commercial Observer reported Monday that M&T Realty Capital provided a $25.5 million interest-only bridge loan for Goldcrest Properties to acquire the 125-unit Hope’s Crossing property in Toms River, New Jersey. That is not a glamorous headline, but it is useful because it shows regional and relationship-oriented bank capital is still available for plain-vanilla apartment business where the basis and sponsorship are understandable. In this market, that kind of ordinary bank deal can be more informative than a flashy one-off trophy financing.

Debt funds remain very much in the game as well. Commercial Observer reported Monday morning that Affinius Capital and Axonic Capital provided a $42.5 million refinance for a two-property self-storage portfolio in Coral Gables and Pembroke Pines. It was their fifth joint origination. The headline is self-storage rather than office or apartments, but the read-through for debt desks is straightforward: private credit is still doing what private credit does best, which is leaning into asset-level complexity, speed and sponsorship familiarity where traditional lenders may not care enough to compete.

Put those deals together and the execution map is pretty clear. Banks can still win straightforward apartment or relationship business. Life company capital will still write large checks, but usually where the sponsorship, location and exit story are unusually clean. Debt funds remain a real source of flexibility. And bridge capital is still the natural answer for office assets that are improved but not yet fully stabilized. That is a healthier market than the one we had at the worst part of the rate shock, but it is still a segmented one.

On the benchmark side, SOFR staying at 3.59 percent is not dramatic by itself, but the combination of a relatively stable overnight base rate with a still-heavy 10-year and 30-year matters. It keeps floating-rate bridge debt workable for borrowers who believe they can create value quickly, while long fixed-rate executions still require more discipline on proceeds and leverage. That is why the market keeps favoring short-to-medium duration decisions instead of locking everything out for a decade just because the calendar says to.

CMBS remains open, but it still wants the cleanest stories. The freshest broad market backdrop from Trepp is that the June CMBS delinquency rate eased to 7.35 percent. That is better at the headline level, but nobody in the market is reading that as a green light for weak collateral. The more durable read is that securitized lenders can execute when cash flow is stable, sponsorship is clear and the asset can survive secondary-market scrutiny. When those conditions are missing, the distress and servicing pipeline still matter more than the improving headline rate.

Multifamily remains the deepest lane, and Monday’s tape reinforced that from several angles. We already mentioned the M&T acquisition financing in Toms River and the huge Miami construction loan. There was also another large residential construction signal on Monday afternoon when Commercial Observer reported that Madison Realty Capital and Cottonwood Group supplied $211 million to build the 112-unit LIDO Asbury Park condominium project on the New Jersey oceanfront. It is condos rather than rental, but it still tells you lenders are willing to fund residential product when the location is irreplaceable and the sponsor story is strong.

Agency activity still matters because it gives the apartment market a steadier outlet than most other property types have. Freddie Mac’s official multifamily certificates calendar shows the K-1811 conventional fixed 10-year deal on the week-of-July-20 schedule with projected issuance size around $1.1 billion. Freddie also announced on Monday a new Multi PC pricing table intended to give investors more timely visibility into participation certificate and Giant PC issuance. That is not a flashy borrower headline, but it is a useful market-structure signal. Freddie is trying to make its multifamily securitization channel more transparent at a moment when investors still care a lot about execution certainty.

Freddie’s earlier July 13 refinance test also still matters in the background. The company said the implied 10-year forward rate in that new test is 5.78 percent. That tells you the agency lane is still underwritten with a sober long-rate assumption, not a rosy one. So yes, the agencies are active, but they are not pretending the refinance environment has become easy.

Fannie Mae’s freshest visible signal is operational rather than transactional. Its Multifamily Guide page shows Guide Update 26-18, covering near-stabilized property submissions, with an effective date of Monday, July 20. That is not a splashy policy swing, but it is still evidence that Fannie is actively tuning its underwriting and delivery framework rather than standing still. For borrowers and lenders, the agency message remains the same: there is liquidity, but it comes with rules, process and discipline.

On HUD and FHA, the biggest useful point today is stability rather than a new splashy announcement. There was not a fresh July 20 or July 21 multifamily policy headline that changed the lane overnight, and that is fine. In the current market, a stable FHA and HUD-backed multifamily channel is itself supportive because it preserves a dependable outlet for affordable and workforce housing even while private lenders stay choosy.

The concise market snapshot this morning is this. The latest verified Treasury close is 4.21 percent on the 2-year, 4.33 percent on the 5-year, 4.60 percent on the 10-year, and 5.11 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.59 percent for July 17. Banks are lending, but mostly where leverage and relationships make sense. Life companies are active, but they are still reserving their best conviction for large, high-clarity stories. Debt funds are handling complexity and transitional business. Office can get financed, but only with a real stabilization story. Multifamily remains the strongest and deepest lane, especially where the agencies or strong residential fundamentals can support the underwriting.

One thing to watch today is whether this week’s residential financing momentum broadens beyond the obvious winners. If we keep seeing bank bridge, life company capital, private credit and agency securitization all show up around apartments and residential-adjacent product, then the market is telling you multifamily liquidity is not just surviving, it is broadening. If the tape narrows back down to only the biggest sponsors and the cleanest coastal stories, then lenders are still picking their spots more carefully than the headline volume might suggest.

The takeaway for Tuesday, July 21, is straightforward. Nationally, the day starts with live storm risk in the Gulf, a food-safety story that still has not settled down, a security incident in lower Manhattan, and a federal government still testing harder legal tools. In Debt Desk, the message is that capital is there, but capital still wants a reason. Duration remains expensive, bridge money remains useful, and multifamily still has the widest and most credible set of execution options in the market.

It is Monday, July 20th, and this is Debt Desk.

National

Let’s start with the national morning brief, because the country is opening this week with a mix of weather risk, legal escalation, and a food-safety story that has moved well beyond a single restaurant chain.

The first story is really two linked weather stories now. South and Central Texas are still in cleanup mode after last week’s flooding, but the weather risk has not fully cleared the map. The Associated Press reported over the weekend that the flooding killed at least two people, triggered hundreds of rescues, and damaged roads, bridges, homes and local business corridors across a broad stretch of the state. Now, as of Monday, July 20, the National Hurricane Center says Tropical Depression Two is lingering near the northern Gulf Coast and could bring more heavy rain along the coast and into parts of the region in the days ahead. That matters because once a market shifts from rescue into cleanup, even moderate additional rain becomes more disruptive than it would have been a week earlier. Crews are trying to restore access, insurers are beginning to size losses, and small businesses are trying to figure out whether they can reopen. So the Texas story is no longer just about dramatic weather footage. It is an infrastructure story, a municipal-stress story, and for lenders and investors, an early read on how quickly damaged local economies can normalize.

The second story is the Justice Department’s decision to activate the Alien Terrorist Removal Court for the first time since Congress created it in 1996. AP reported today, July 20, that the administration filed its first petition into that dormant court and that the judge immediately asked for more information after an initial hearing. The legal details matter, but the broader signal matters more. This is a reminder that the administration is still searching for harder-edged immigration tools and is willing to test little-used authorities if it thinks traditional channels are too slow or too exposed. That does not directly move a swap rate this morning, but it does add to the sense that Washington is operating in a more experimental, more confrontational posture. Markets do not ignore that kind of shift forever, especially when it shapes labor, enforcement risk, and political noise.

The third story is food safety, and it widened materially in the last twenty-four hours. AP reported Sunday, July 19, that Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled iceberg lettuce products shipped to 27 states after federal investigators tied cyclospora illnesses to lettuce served at Taco Bell in five states. That is important because the story has moved from one branded point of sale to a broader supply-chain issue. Once a recall jumps into multiple states and multiple product codes, it becomes a confidence story as much as a public-health story. Consumers pull back first, then operators start auditing sourcing, and then distributors and landlords start watching foot traffic and tenant performance more carefully if the problem lingers. It is not systemically important on its own, but it is another example of how a concentrated operating problem can spread nationally in very little time.

The fourth story is the smoke story, which is easing but not finished. AP reported Sunday that thunderstorms were expected to clear much of the wildfire smoke that had hung over the Northeast just in time for major outdoor events, but the last few days made clear that this is not a fringe environmental headline anymore. Air quality disruptions already hit sports schedules, outdoor activity, and basic day-to-day operating conditions across large East Coast and Midwest markets. Even if the haze improves this morning, the practical lesson remains the same: wildfire smoke is now a recurring business interruption risk, not a once-in-a-summer anomaly. It affects consumer behavior, outdoor labor, event economics, and even simple assumptions about when a city is fully open for business.

So the national setup for Monday is pretty straightforward. Texas is recovering while still exposed to additional rainfall risk. Washington is testing a new legal lane on immigration. The produce recall story is broader and messier than it first looked. And the smoke may be thinning, but the operating lesson from it is not going away. That is the backdrop for the debt conversation this morning.

Debt Desk

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor is rates, and the numbers are verified. As of this Monday morning run, the latest official Treasury close is Friday, July 17. The curve closed at 4.18 percent on the 2-year, 4.28 percent on the 5-year, 4.55 percent on the 10-year, and 5.06 percent on the 30-year, according to the U.S. Treasury. The latest official SOFR print is 3.59 percent for July 17, according to the New York Fed.

That curve is worth sitting with for a minute, because the shape matters as much as the level. The front end has come in enough to keep shorter-duration fixed-rate debt and floating-rate structures alive, but the long end is still doing real damage to proceeds once you layer on lender spread, reserves, and structure. A 10-year at 4.55 percent is not a crisis print. A 30-year at 5.06 percent still feels heavy, especially for borrowers who need full-term certainty and do not have the cushion to absorb a wider all-in coupon. In plain English, money is more workable than it was when both the curve and spreads were punishing borrowers at the same time, but it is still not easy. That is why five-year money, hybrid structures, and transitional executions continue to matter so much.

That also helps explain why lender behavior is still segmented rather than broadly reopened. Banks can lend, but they do not have to pretend they are hungry across every product type. Life companies can still stay selective because long-duration capital remains valuable and the long bond is giving them cover to demand discipline. CMBS is available, but only where the collateral is clean enough to survive securitized scrutiny. And debt funds remain relevant because a lot of borrowers still need speed, flexibility, or tolerance for business-plan complexity that traditional lenders do not want to warehouse.

You can see that in the latest office-adjacent financing tape. Commercial Observer reported on July 17 that Hudson Bay Capital provided a $60 million bridge refinance for the Bell Works Fort Monmouth campus in Tinton Falls, New Jersey. This is not a generic office story. It is a repurposed mixed-use campus story with visible leasing momentum, occupancy around the high-eighties, and a headline tenant narrative anchored by Jersey Mike’s planned headquarters move. That distinction matters. Capital is still not broadly saying yes to office. It is saying yes when the sponsor can show that the property has already crossed the hard part of the bridge from obsolete space into a functioning mixed-use ecosystem with cash flow and a credible next chapter.

Bank balance-sheet tone remains selective as well. Trepp’s latest CRE debt work, highlighted this past week, shows overall debt growth improving, but with a very important split under the surface. The median bank is still adding CRE exposure, including some construction balances, while the largest banks continue pulling back enough to keep the aggregate picture restrained. That is the part borrowers need to hear clearly. There is debt available, but a few successful deals do not equal a broad reopening of construction appetite. If you are bringing a bank a relationship deal with good deposits, low leverage, and a clean sponsorship story, you have a lane. If you are asking for higher-leverage speculative exposure, the lane is still much narrower.

CMBS is telling a similar story. Trepp’s June delinquency data showed the headline CMBS delinquency rate improving to 7.35 percent, but that better headline sits next to continuing stress in the workout pipeline and elevated distress across major markets. Commercial Observer’s recent CRED iQ coverage showed overall CMBS distress among the 25 largest U.S. metro areas at 12.7 percent in May, with much sharper pain in certain office-heavy metros. So the right read is not that CMBS has turned easy. The right read is that the market is open for assets that can handle hard underwriting, while problem assets are still very much a servicing and maturity story.

That is why execution tone today still breaks out pretty cleanly by lender type. Banks want relationship business and defendable leverage. Life companies want durable income and minimal narrative risk. CMBS wants collateral that can travel well and survive secondary-market scrutiny. Debt funds want to be paid for complexity, transition, or time-sensitive closings. None of that is especially new, but the current curve is not forcing those lines to blur. If anything, it is keeping them in place.

Multifamily remains the deepest pool for real activity, and the last several days reinforced that from a few different angles at once. Commercial Observer reported July 17 that Ponce Bank provided $50 million of construction financing for two contiguous apartment buildings in Canarsie totaling 198 units. The deal closed July 13, and a portion of the units will qualify for New York’s 485-x tax-abatement program. That matters because it shows where construction credit still clears: apartments, policy support, a local housing-supply argument, and a basis lenders can defend without getting heroic. Construction money is still selective, but it is absolutely not absent when the story lines up.

Affordable housing capital also stayed active. Commercial Observer reported July 17 that Greystone Real Estate Capital closed its second affordable housing development fund at $137 million of LIHTC equity, aimed at nearly 2,000 units across 20 properties in nine states. That is not just an equity headline. It is a credit signal. Institutional capital is still willing to fund affordable housing at scale because the policy framework, tenant demand, and mission alignment remain easier to explain than a lot of market-rate development risk. For the multifamily stack overall, that means affordability continues to act as both a social objective and a capital-market advantage.

There was also a meaningful CMBS print inside multifamily. Commercial Observer reported July 17 that Citi priced an $816.9 million multifamily-only conduit transaction backed by 27 five-year interest-only loans, the largest single-bank-contributed multifamily-only conduit deal since the global financial crisis. That matters for two reasons. First, it tells you investor demand for apartment collateral remains real, not theoretical. Second, it reinforces how much the securitized market still prefers product types with stable cash flow and a simpler credit story. That deal does not mean every apartment borrower gets a wide-open conduit lane, but it does say the market will reward clean multifamily pools with sharper execution than many other property types can get right now.

Agency activity remains part of the stabilizing picture too. Freddie Mac’s official multifamily certificates calendar shows its K-1811 conventional fixed 10-year deal scheduled for announcement the week of Monday, July 20, with projected issuance size around $1.1 billion. That is not a final priced transaction yet, but it is still useful because it shows the agency securitization machine remains active and visible right into this week. In a market where borrowers care about dependable exits, that steady agency pipeline matters. Fannie Mae’s platform message remains similar. Its multifamily business continues to emphasize DUS execution, affordable housing, and green financing as the cleanest lanes for steady liquidity.

Trepp’s latest agency credit numbers back that up. Its July 17 update showed total securitized agency multifamily delinquency at just 0.47 percent in May, with Fannie Mae at 0.24 percent, Freddie Mac at 0.87 percent, and Ginnie Mae, FHA, and HUD at 0.51 percent. Freddie still runs somewhat higher, but the broader point is stability. Agency credit is not flashing stress in a way that would force a change in lender posture. It is still one of the cleanest parts of the broader CRE credit picture.

On HUD and FHA specifically, the freshest headline this morning is not a brand-new policy announcement. The more important read is that the federally backed multifamily channel still looks stable in the data, and that matters because it helps preserve confidence in the deeper affordable and workforce-housing lane even when private construction lending remains selective. In this market, no bad surprise from HUD or FHA-backed credit is itself useful information.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The latest verified Treasury close is 4.18 percent on the 2-year, 4.28 percent on the 5-year, 4.55 percent on the 10-year, and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. The latest verified SOFR print is 3.59 percent. Bank appetite is better than it was, but large banks still are not broadly embracing construction risk. Office debt is getting done mainly where the repositioning story is already real. CMBS is functioning, but only for collateral that can stand up to tough underwriting. Multifamily remains the strongest lane, especially where affordability, agencies, or clean securitization fit are involved.

One thing to watch this week is whether multifamily liquidity keeps broadening from multiple directions at once. If we keep seeing apartment construction loans, affordable-housing equity raises, agency securitization, and multifamily-only conduit execution all show up together, then the right read is that lenders are extending comfort beyond just one narrow lane of apartment credit. If that follow-through stalls, then the market is still clustering around the single easiest collateral to defend rather than truly reopening.

The takeaway for this Monday is straightforward. Nationally, the week starts with live weather risk in Texas, a sharper legal posture out of Washington, a broader-than-expected food recall, and another reminder that environmental disruptions can hit major markets fast. In Debt Desk, the market is open, but it still rewards specificity. Borrowers can get debt, but the cleanest executions are still going to assets lenders already trust, capital stacks they can explain to committees, and business plans that do not depend on optimism carrying the underwriting. That remains most true in multifamily, selectively true in high-conviction adaptive-reuse office, and much less true anywhere the story still needs to be rescued after closing.

It is Sunday, July 19th, and this is Debt Desk.

National

Let’s start with the national morning brief, because the backdrop this weekend is a mix of cleanup, public-health disruption, and a federal policy posture that is getting more assertive in very visible ways.

The biggest continuity story is still Texas, but the angle has shifted. The Associated Press reported on July 18 that catastrophic flooding across South and Central Texas had killed at least two people, forced hundreds of rescues, damaged roads and bridges, and left communities from Uvalde outward trying to figure out what normal even looks like after days of relentless rain. That matters because the real economic impact of a flood rarely shows up in the first headline. It shows up when stores stay closed, medicine is hard to find, bridges stay offline, and families start counting what was lost inside homes and small businesses. So this is not just a weather story this morning. It is now an infrastructure, insurance and local-credit story, and it will stay that way into the coming week.

The second story is the air itself across the Northeast. AP reported this morning, July 19, that thunderstorms were expected to clear much of the wildfire smoke that has drifted in from Canada and Minnesota, after haze pushed into major East Coast markets and turned parts of the region gray for days. The improvement is meaningful, but it does not erase what the last stretch has shown. Wildfire smoke has become an operating condition, not just an environmental headline. It can change event planning, outdoor work, travel comfort, public-health guidance and consumer behavior in real time. Even when the air improves, the lesson for businesses and local governments is the same: this kind of disruption is showing up more often, and it does not respect regional boundaries.

The third story is out of Washington, where AP reported today that the Justice Department has activated the Alien Terrorist Removal Court for the first time since Congress created it in 1996. The court had never been used until the administration filed a petition on Wednesday, and the judge overseeing the matter has already asked the government for additional information after an initial hearing. The immediate significance is legal and procedural, but the broader significance is political and institutional. It tells you the administration is still looking for harder-edged immigration tools and is willing to test dormant authorities if it thinks the existing system is too slow or too exposed to public process. Markets are not repricing office loans because of one immigration court filing, but they do register when federal enforcement posture becomes more aggressive and more experimental.

The fourth story is a consumer health story with national reach. AP reported today that federal investigators traced lettuce served at Taco Bell locations in five states to a cyclospora outbreak. That is not on the same scale as a national disaster or a major policy fight, but it does matter because it hits a lot of the same themes that keep showing up across the economy right now: supply-chain quality control, public confidence, and how quickly a localized problem becomes a multi-state issue once a large national brand is involved. For consumers it is a practical warning. For operators it is another reminder that even an otherwise stable summer demand backdrop can be interrupted by one contamination event.

So the national setup this Sunday is pretty clear. Texas is moving from rescue into a long cleanup. The smoke story may be easing, but it is still a live sign of environmental disruption spilling into daily business. Washington is testing more aggressive legal machinery on immigration. And public-health risk has jumped back into the headlines through a national restaurant chain. That is the atmosphere borrowers, lenders and investors are walking into today.

Debt Desk

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor is rates, and the numbers are verified. As of this Sunday morning run, the latest official Treasury close is Friday, July 17. The curve closed at 4.18 percent on the 2-year, 4.28 percent on the 5-year, 4.55 percent on the 10-year and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.62 percent for July 16, according to the New York Fed.

The front end is no bargain, yet it is restrained enough to keep shorter fixed-rate structures and floating-rate executions in the conversation. The long end is the heavier part of the stack. A 10-year in the mid-fours is workable in theory, but the 30-year above 5 percent keeps long-duration money expensive once lender spread, reserves and structure get layered in. In plain English, borrowers still are not choosing between cheap money and expensive money. They are choosing between manageable pain and more durable pain, and that keeps five-year thinking very alive.

That also explains why lender behavior still feels segmented instead of unified. Banks can make the case for disciplined relationship lending and modest leverage because they are not being forced to chase volume. Life companies can still demand a premium for long-duration certainty because the long bond is doing some of that work for them. Debt funds can keep selling flexibility, speed and complexity capital because plenty of borrowers still cannot fit a pristine permanent-loan box. And CMBS remains open, but with the usual condition that the asset and the narrative both have to survive unforgiving underwriting.

You can see that in the week’s office-adjacent financing tape. Commercial Observer reported July 18 that Hudson Bay Capital provided a $60 million refinance for the Bell Works Fort Monmouth campus in Tinton Falls, New Jersey. The deal matters because it is not really a vote of confidence in generic office. It is a vote for a very specific kind of office-adjacent story: reuse, mixed-use character, and a tangible tenancy narrative, including Jersey Mike’s planned headquarters presence. That is the distinction lenders continue to make. Capital is not broadly saying yes to office. It is saying yes to office when the building has already moved meaningfully away from plain-vanilla office risk.

Trepp’s July 17 bank-lending work lines up with that same selective tone. Its latest analysis showed aggregate CRE loan growth improving, but the weakness is still concentrated at the largest banks, especially in construction. The median bank is still adding exposure, including in construction, while the biggest institutions remain the ones pulling balances down enough to drag the aggregate. That is a useful reality check because it keeps borrowers from overreading a few positive deals. There is credit out there, but it is not the same thing as broad reopening. Cleaner sponsorship, better basis, stronger deposits, and lower leverage still matter a lot if you are asking a bank to show up.

CMBS is sending a similarly mixed but usable signal. That combination is important. It says some loans are curing or resolving, but fresh stress is still moving into the workout channel. So securitization is available, yet it remains judgmental. The market is open, but it does not want hand-waving. If a borrower needs conduit execution, the deal still has to read cleanly from cash flow through rollover through refinanceability.

That discipline is one reason the lender stack today still looks pretty consistent. Banks want relationship business and cleaner stories. Life companies want stabilized assets and very little narrative drama. CMBS wants collateral that can travel through securitized underwriting without heroic assumptions. Debt funds want to be paid for speed, complexity or transitional business plans. None of that is new, but it remains the operating map because the curve and the credit data are not forcing a new hierarchy yet.

Multifamily is still the strongest lane, and this week’s flow backed that up from several angles at once. Commercial Observer reported July 18 that Ponce Bank supplied a $50 million construction loan for a 198-unit apartment project in Canarsie. The 485-x tax-abatement structure and affordable component matter here because they help explain why apartment construction can still clear when other projects stall. Construction capital is selective, but apartments with policy support, workable basis and a defined local demand story still have a path.

The affordable-housing capital story stayed active as well. Institutional capital still wants affordable housing exposure, and that continues to support the parts of multifamily that come with mission alignment, durable subsidy structures and clearer policy support.

Commercial Observer reported July 17 that Citi priced an $816.9 million all-multifamily conduit transaction made up of 27 five-year interest-only loans, the largest single-bank-contributed multifamily-only conduit deal since the global financial crisis. The AAA bonds priced at swaps plus 80 basis points, tighter than the comparable multifamily cash-flow execution earlier this year. That does not mean every apartment borrower suddenly has a wider-open securitized lane. But it does suggest that investors still want apartment collateral badly enough to support sharper execution when the pool is clean.

Trepp’s July 17 agency credit update reinforces that backdrop. Total securitized agency delinquency improved to 0.47 percent in May, with Fannie Mae at 0.24 percent, Freddie Mac at 0.87 percent and Ginnie Mae, FHA and HUD at 0.51 percent. Freddie still runs higher, but Trepp’s explanation is that structure and maturity treatment are still doing some of the work there rather than a broad deterioration in apartment credit. The bigger point is that multifamily credit performance inside the agency universe still looks steady enough to keep lenders comfortable.

On HUD and FHA specifically, I did not find a fresh multifamily execution or policy development published in the last 24 hours strong enough to lead as a standalone Sunday headline. But the Ginnie Mae, FHA and HUD delinquency reading still matters because it says the federally backed multifamily credit channel remains fundamentally stable, even if the newest visible momentum this week came more from banks, LIHTC equity, Fannie execution and apartment CMBS.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The latest verified Treasury close is 4.18 percent on the 2-year, 4.28 percent on the 5-year, 4.55 percent on the 10-year and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. The latest verified SOFR print is 3.62 percent. Bank appetite is improving, but large banks are still not embracing construction risk in a broad way. Office financing exists mainly where a real reuse or tenancy story is already in place. CMBS is functioning, but still selective. Multifamily remains the deepest and cleanest pool for execution, especially where agencies, affordability structures or strong securitization fit are involved.

One thing to watch this week is whether the apartment capital stack keeps opening from multiple directions at once. If more multifamily-only CMBS, agency refinancings and affordable-housing capital raises print behind this week’s deals, then the read will be that lenders are getting more comfortable expanding around the strongest property type. If the follow-through is thin, then this week may end up looking more like concentration than reopening, with capital still clustering around the easiest collateral to defend.

The takeaway for this Sunday is straightforward. Nationally, the country is dealing with a cleanup story in Texas, a still-live environmental disruption story in the Northeast, a sharper federal enforcement story in Washington, and a new consumer health warning. In Debt Desk, the market is open, but it still demands specificity. Borrowers can get debt, but the cleanest executions are still going to assets lenders already trust, structures they can explain to committees, and stories they do not have to rescue after closing.
