The third story is a fresh institutional confrontation out of Seattle. AP reported that President Donald Trump fired the newly court-appointed top federal prosecutor in Seattle less than an hour after federal judges in the district unanimously appointed him. The immediate significance is narrow, but the larger signal is not. It is another example of how fights over appointments, legal authority and executive control are moving from background process stories into front-page operating stories. When that keeps happening, it affects how markets think about policy execution, litigation timelines and regulatory certainty.

The fourth story is tonight’s White House address. AP reported that Trump is expected to use a primetime address to focus on election issues and to revisit claims tied to past voting disputes. Whether the speech actually lands as a major policy moment or as another political provocation, the build-up matters. It tells you the administration wants election administration and election legitimacy back near the center of the national conversation heading toward the midterms. For investors and lenders, that does not price directly into debt costs this morning. But it does shape the broader volatility backdrop, especially if the speech triggers legal, legislative or state-level responses.

The fifth story is the immigration enforcement backlash building around the Department of Homeland Security. AP reported Wednesday that Trump said ICE should keep making traffic stops despite internal moves to limit them after a series of fatal encounters. That keeps the story alive because it is no longer just about a tragic set of incidents. It is also about whether agency leadership can change tactics when political pressure runs the other direction. For markets, that kind of friction matters because it becomes another measure of how consistently federal agencies can operate under pressure.

So the national setup this morning is a mix of physical disruption and political strain. Flooding is active in Texas. Smoke and heat are combining across a wider slice of the country. The White House is opening a new front in the election conversation. Immigration enforcement remains under scrutiny. And the fight over control of federal offices is getting more public, not less.

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor, as always, is rates. As of this Thursday morning run, the latest verified official Treasury close is from Wednesday, July 15. The curve closed at 4.13 percent on the 2-year, 4.26 percent on the 5-year, 4.55 percent on the 10-year and 5.08 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.63 percent for Tuesday, July 14. Freddie Mac’s latest weekly primary mortgage market survey still shows the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 6.49 percent for the week ending July 9.

That curve tells a more useful story than the 10-year alone. The front end eased a bit with softer recent inflation data, but it is still high enough that floating-rate debt is not a casual choice. The 5-year remains the practical center of gravity for a lot of real borrower decisions, because it still offers a better pain trade than going all the way out the curve. And the 30-year staying above 5 percent keeps full-duration life company money expensive enough that many borrowers still prefer to compromise on tenor rather than pay for the longest lane.

In other words, the market is offering structure, not relief. Borrowers can get certainty, but they still have to choose carefully where they want to pay for it.

That is showing up in the latest deal flow. Commercial Observer reported July 15 that RXR, Waterfall Asset Management and New York Life provided $103 million for the recapitalization of Andalex Group’s Sylvan Corporate Center medical campus in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey. It is not a plain office story and that is exactly why it matters. Capital is still showing clear preference for property types with stronger tenancy durability and more defensible demand. Medical office and healthcare-adjacent product continue to attract money because the cash-flow story is easier to underwrite than generic office.

The broader office lesson still comes from the divide inside the sector. Trepp’s July 14 analysis of what it called bifurcating office performance reinforced that capital is separating buildings that can still refinance from buildings that cannot. That lines up with the continuity story already on our tracker from Manhattan and Washington office financings earlier this week. Good offices are financeable. Proven turnarounds can reach permanent debt. But the market is still deeply skeptical of assets that have weak leasing, functional obsolescence or uncertain capex demands.

CMBS is open, but it is not forgiving. Trepp reported on July 13 that the CMBS special servicing rate rose 34 basis points in June to 11.20 percent, reversing the prior month’s decline, even as the June delinquency rate had separately improved to 7.35 percent. That combination is important. It says resolution is still happening, but stress is not gone. Some loans are curing, some are being worked through, and new trouble is still arriving. The headline for borrowers is that conduit execution exists, but scrutiny remains intense and spreads still need to compensate lenders for property-specific uncertainty.

That leaves the lender stack in a fairly coherent place this morning. Banks are lending, but still favoring relationship business, lower leverage and cleaner sponsorship stories. Life companies remain interested in stabilized, lower-leverage product, particularly when the borrower wants quality execution and can tolerate the cost of duration. CMBS is functioning best where the asset can survive securitized underwriting without too much narrative risk. Debt funds continue to fill the gap wherever the plan includes construction, lease-up, transition or some other complexity that traditional lenders would rather avoid.

The market is not closed. It is selective, disciplined and still charging heavily for ambiguity.

Multifamily remains the deepest lane, and the freshest visible evidence is still constructive. Commercial Observer reported July 15 that Slate Property Group and RiseBoro Community Partnership landed roughly $163 million of financing for two Williamsburg housing projects that will deliver 312 affordable apartments. That is a useful signal because it shows capital continuing to support affordable and mission-oriented apartment development even while broader construction lending remains selective. If a project has a strong public-policy angle, a defined takeout story and credible sponsorship, money can still line up.

There is another smaller but telling construction datapoint from Philadelphia. Commercial Observer reported July 14 that S3 Capital provided a $24 million construction loan to Ampere Capital Group for a 109-unit mixed-use apartment project in Fishtown. That is not a megadeal, but it helps confirm that debt funds are still active in the urban multifamily development lane where the sponsor, submarket and basis make sense. This is one of the clearest patterns in the market right now: banks are not absent, but nonbank lenders are still doing a lot of the work where flexibility matters.

And that fits the broader multifamily capital-markets story. Connect CRE reported July 15, citing Yardi Matrix, that private equity is increasingly using debt investments to gain apartment exposure because property sales remain relatively muted. The same report said debt funds are taking a bigger share of the market, agency lenders Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have expanded securitization offerings, and multifamily-only CMBS pools are starting to come back. That is a concise description of how capital is adapting. If equity buyers do not love today’s pricing and rate backdrop, they can still express conviction through debt.

Agency activity remains one of the cleanest permanent-debt answers in the market. That was true earlier this week with the Northmarq Fannie Mae execution in Massachusetts and the Merchants Capital Freddie Mac affordable-housing deal in Kansas, and it remains true this morning as the broader tape develops. The agencies still look like the most dependable long-term debt lane for stabilized multifamily, especially where affordability, occupancy and sponsorship are easy to defend.

Freddie Mac’s own platform signals support that view. Its integrated Conventional Small product for loans under $10 million, announced this year, is another reminder that the agency wants to stay relevant across a wider borrower base, not just the largest institutional deals. Fannie Mae’s July-effective guide updates on insurance and servicing mechanics tell a similar story. These are not flashy headlines, but they are the sort of operating signals that matter when you are judging whether an origination channel is alive, current and still trying to reduce avoidable friction.

HUD and FHA are quieter again this morning. I did not find a fresh multifamily closing or policy headline from HUD or FHA published within the last 24 hours strong enough to carry as a primary item. So for now, the public tape remains more active around debt funds, local construction lenders and the agencies than around HUD-led multifamily execution.

The multifamily CMBS story is also worth keeping in frame. Apartments still price better than office in conduit markets, but that does not mean apartment underwriting is loose. The market still prefers in-place occupancy, realistic expense assumptions and business plans that do not depend on heroic rent growth. Borrowers who bought into aggressive value-add assumptions a few years ago still face real refinance friction even in the strongest property type.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The latest verified Treasury close is 4.13 percent on the 2-year, 4.26 percent on the 5-year, 4.55 percent on the 10-year and 5.08 percent on the 30-year. The latest verified SOFR print is 3.63 percent. Mortgage rates remain high enough that housing turnover stays constrained, which still supports rental demand even if rent growth is modest. Healthcare-oriented commercial assets are still finding lender support. Office remains bifurcated. CMBS is open but judgmental. Debt funds are still solving for construction and transition risk. And agency multifamily debt remains one of the cleanest lanes in the market.

One thing to watch today is whether the recent move lower in the front end of the Treasury curve actually changes borrower behavior or just makes existing preferences more obvious. If the 2-year keeps easing while the 30-year stays stubbornly high, that still argues for five- to seven-year fixed-rate structures as the most practical compromise. If that dynamic holds, life companies should stay selective, banks should keep protecting proceeds, CMBS should remain disciplined on spreads, and debt funds should continue to win the assignments where certainty and flexibility matter more than price alone.

The takeaway for this Thursday is straightforward. Nationally, the country is dealing with active weather disruption, environmental stress and another round of institutional conflict. In Debt Desk, capital is present, but it still expects borrowers to arrive with clarity. Multifamily remains the strongest financing lane, especially where affordability and stabilization are easy to prove. CMBS is functioning, though hardly loose. Office is still a tale of two markets. And the curve continues to say the same thing it has been saying for weeks: structure matters, duration is expensive, and there is still no free money in this market.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk Morning Brief for July 13, 2026
item.description: A dangerous U.S. heat wave, Missouri flood rescues, a sharp press-freedom clash, and election-administration uncertainty lead the national morning brief before Debt Desk turns to the latest Treasury and SOFR prints, office and multifamily financings, CMBS execution tone, agency signals, and one thing to watch for Monday, July 13, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
It is Monday, July 13th, and this is Debt Desk.

Let’s start with the national morning brief, because the country is opening the week with a familiar pattern: the biggest stories are operating stories. They affect how people move, how agencies function and how risk gets priced.

The first story this morning is the heat. The Associated Press first published on Saturday, July 11, and updated on Sunday, July 12, that a widespread and dangerous heat wave is pressing across much of the United States under a strong heat dome, with triple-digit temperatures in parts of the West and Plains before the system pushes farther east. AP reported that more than 90 local temperature records could be tied or broken through midweek, with many of those records on the overnight side. That matters because hot nights turn the story into a stress test for power systems, outdoor labor, public health operations, logistics and household budgets.

The second story is flood damage and emergency response in Missouri. AP first published on Saturday, July 11, and updated that story over the weekend after floodwaters forced helicopter rescues from a summer camp, left one woman dead, and shut down roads as the Black River continued rising. It is another reminder that climate and catastrophe risk keep moving from tail event toward regular operating backdrop, which matters for insurers, municipal issuers, utilities and lenders underwriting local durability.

The third story is still the administration’s pressure campaign against the press. AP first published on Friday, July 11, and updated over the weekend that the Department of Justice subpoenaed New York Times reporters over their reporting on security concerns tied to the Qatari-gifted Air Force One. The article says the subpoenas would force testimony before a federal grand jury in Manhattan this week. For markets, this is another sign that information risk, legal process risk and reputational risk are increasingly entangled.

The fourth story is election administration. AP published on Friday, July 10, that President Donald Trump removed Democratic members of the Election Assistance Commission, the federal body that helps distribute election grants, test voting systems and maintain the national voter registration form. That is an important story not because markets trade every agency staffing move, but because this one bears directly on how a critical national process is administered ahead of the midterms. If legal challenges or appointment delays keep the commission unstable, then grants, certifications and procedural confidence all become more fragile. This is exactly the kind of institutional story that can stay in the background right up until some practical deadline makes it suddenly important.

The fifth story is the national housing backdrop. Freddie Mac’s weekly mortgage survey, released Thursday, July 9, put the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 6.49 percent. AP’s housing coverage from Friday, July 11, also pointed to slowing existing-home sales and a record median home price. That still leaves turnover constrained and affordability stressed, which is one reason multifamily demand still has structural support.

So that is the national setup for Monday morning. A large swath of the country is overheating, parts of the Midwest are cleaning up from flood rescues, the federal government is escalating a confrontation with major news organizations, election administration is looking less settled than it should, and housing affordability still is not easing in a meaningful way. None of that shuts the market. But all of it adds friction.

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor, as always, is rates. As of this Monday morning run, the latest official Treasury close available is from Friday, July 10. The U.S. Treasury curve closed at 4.21 percent on the 2-year, 4.30 percent on the 5-year, 4.56 percent on the 10-year and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print available from the New York Fed is 3.53 percent for Thursday, July 9. Freddie Mac’s average 30-year mortgage rate, again for the week ending July 9, is 6.49 percent.

That is still a workable market, but it is not an easy one. The front end remains high enough that floating-rate debt still needs to be justified, not defaulted into. A 3.53 SOFR print does not sound terrible in isolation, but once spread, cap cost, reserves and extension assumptions are layered in, the carry is still meaningful. The 2-year Treasury tells you floating money is not cheap enough to be casual. The 5-year tells you why so much real fixed-rate execution keeps clustering in the middle of the curve. And the 30-year tells you why long-duration life company money remains expensive enough that only certain borrowers truly want it.

Looking only at the 10-year misses too much. Many actual borrower decisions are being made somewhere between the 2-year and the 7-year, with the 5-year acting as the practical center of gravity. The curve is not telling borrowers that all-in debt is attractive. It is telling them that the middle lanes remain the least painful.

The clearest large office refinancing datapoint still comes from Manhattan. JLL announced on Thursday, July 9, that it arranged a $352 million floating-rate SASB refinancing for 425 Lexington Avenue through Goldman Sachs, fully pre-placed with funds and accounts managed by BlackRock. That is an important transaction because it says institutional office liquidity is absolutely there for the right product, but also that the market is still highly selective about what counts as financeable office. This is a 99 percent leased, heavily upgraded, Grand Central-adjacent tower. In other words, this is not a generic office reopening story. It is a proof-of-liquidity story for elite collateral.

That deal matters beyond one tower because it shows how execution is happening. The financing was curated, structured and pre-placed with serious institutional capital. If the building is first-rate, the tenant story is strong and the sponsor is credible, large office debt can get done. If those elements weaken, the market becomes much thinner very quickly.

There is also a smaller but useful office CMBS signal from Washington. Commercial Observer reported on Friday, July 10, that Jemal Equities refinanced 1750 H Street NW with a $27 million CMBS loan from Citibank arranged by Meridian Capital Group. That building was almost fully vacant when Jemal bought it in July 2025, but the report says it saw leasing momentum strong enough to take out the bridge debt with fixed-rate permanent financing. That matters because it shows the conduit market is still willing to finance office outside the absolute trophy tier when a real leasing story has already been proven. The takeaway is not that office has become easy. The takeaway is that office can still move from transitional to permanent capital if execution risk has already been burned down.

That lines up with the broader CMBS backdrop. Trepp reported on July 10 that the June CMBS delinquency rate fell 20 basis points to 7.35 percent, helped by a large lodging cure. Trepp’s recent conduit analysis makes the more useful point: five-year conduit loans have become the market’s default setting, while spreads remain disciplined and office still prices wider than multifamily.

So the CMBS read this morning is fairly straightforward. The market is open. It is functioning. It is not in retreat. But it is rewarding discipline, medium-duration structures and collateral quality. Borrowers who still think the conduit market is back in its old form are reading the tape incorrectly.

That brings us to execution tone across the lender stack. Banks are still in the market, but they remain selective on leverage, sponsorship and relationship value. Life companies remain credible for stabilized, lower-leverage product, but a 30-year Treasury north of 5 percent means that duration comes at a visible cost. CMBS is working where the asset can survive securitized scrutiny. Debt funds remain the flexibility providers wherever the assignment includes construction, lease-up or recapitalization complexity.

In other words, the capital stack has breadth, but not much tolerance for ambiguity. The market is not closed. It is judgmental.

Multifamily remains the deepest lane in that stack, and the freshest headline there is still the July 10 Dwight Mortgage Trust construction loan in Gilroy, California. Connect CRE reported that Dwight provided a $183 million construction loan for a 530-unit multifamily development, the largest construction financing in the company’s history. That is a significant debt-fund signal. It shows that apartment construction is still one of the few property types capable of attracting large-scale floating-rate development capital when the sponsor, submarket and affordability profile make sense. The deal includes both market-rate townhomes and income-restricted units, which matters because mixed-income and workforce-oriented stories continue to align better with today’s capital preferences than purely speculative luxury development.

That Dwight financing also says something broader about where risk is being warehoused. Banks have pulled back from many construction assignments. Debt funds have not disappeared from the lane. They have simply gotten more selective and more expensive.

Agency activity remains one of the cleanest permanent-debt answers for stabilized apartments. Connect CRE’s July 9 report on Northmarq’s $22.855 million Fannie Mae DUS acquisition financing for Elora Flats and Townhomes in Lawrence, Massachusetts is still worth carrying because it captures the tone of the agency market very well. The deal came with a seven-year term and four years of interest-only payments on a property that was 100 percent mission-driven and had maintained high occupancy. That is exactly the kind of file the agencies can still handle with confidence: steady cash flow, clear affordability profile, proven performance, and a structure that gives the borrower enough breathing room without pretending leverage is free.

Freddie Mac also remains visibly active, even when the public tape is showing more policy than closings. Freddie Mac Multifamily published its insurance update on July 7, describing changes meant to align requirements and improve consistency. That is not a splashy financing announcement, but it matters operationally. When agency platforms are refining insurance standards instead of freezing them, that is a sign that the machine is active, current and still trying to reduce avoidable friction for borrowers and servicers.

On the Freddie closing side, Connect CRE reported on July 9 that Merchants Capital secured a $10.8 million Freddie Mac Unfunded Forward TEL loan for Floret Hill, a 121-unit affordable housing development in Lawrence, Kansas. That is a smaller transaction than the Dwight construction headline, but it is useful because it shows Freddie still has a clear lane in affordable multifamily execution, especially where public support, tax credit equity and agency debt fit together in a coherent capital stack.

Fannie Mae’s own guide updates remain part of the story too. The Multifamily Guide shows Guide Update 26-16 on insurance became effective July 6. Again, that is not the kind of item you lead a show with, but for active borrowers and lenders it is exactly the kind of operational signal that says agency channels remain open and engaged.

HUD and FHA are quieter again this morning. I did not find a fresh multifamily closing or policy development from HUD or FHA published within the last 24 hours strong enough to carry as a lead item. That means the visible momentum on the public tape right now is sitting more with debt funds and the agencies than with HUD-driven headlines.

The multifamily CMBS read is also worth a quick note. Apartments still price better than office in the conduit market, and Trepp’s spread work makes that clear, but multifamily is not frictionless. Older value-add assumptions, tighter refinance proceeds and higher operating costs still complicate takeouts for some borrowers. So yes, apartment remains the most financeable major property type. But even here, the market is rewarding in-place cash flow and realistic leverage more than optimistic underwriting.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The latest official Treasury close is 4.21 percent on the 2-year, 4.30 percent on the 5-year, 4.56 percent on the 10-year and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.53 percent. Freddie Mac’s 30-year mortgage average is 6.49 percent. Trophy office can refinance if the asset is undeniably strong. Select office CMBS deals can still clear. Five-year conduit structures remain the market’s default format. Debt funds are still winning meaningful multifamily construction assignments. Agency permanent debt remains one of the cleanest ways through the market for stabilized apartment collateral.

One thing to watch this week is whether more borrowers continue choosing the middle of the curve rather than either floating longer or paying up for full duration. If the 5-year Treasury stays well inside the 30-year and SOFR remains sticky, then five- to seven-year fixed-rate executions should keep looking like the most rational compromise in the market. If that dynamic holds, expect life companies to stay selective, CMBS to keep favoring medium-duration structures, banks to protect proceeds, and debt funds to remain the solution set for more dynamic business plans.

The takeaway for this Monday is simple. Nationally, the country is starting the week with heat stress, flood damage, institutional friction and stubborn housing costs. In Debt Desk, capital is available, but it still charges for uncertainty. Office debt is open for the best buildings and for select proven turnarounds. Multifamily remains the strongest lane, especially where affordability, occupancy and sponsorship are easy to defend. The agencies are active. Debt funds matter. And the curve is still telling borrowers that structure matters more than hope.

If that commission is pulled deeper into litigation or simply left without a stable bipartisan structure, the issue stops being abstract almost immediately. It becomes an operating story about grants, certifications, timelines and trust in the machinery itself. Markets do not need an opinion on the politics to care about the execution risk.

Put together, that is still the same uncomfortable national equation: activity is sluggish, borrowing costs are elevated, but prices remain high enough to keep affordability badly strained. For this audience, that is not just a single-family story. It is one of the core reasons multifamily demand remains durable and why apartment finance continues to command more lender attention than most other property types.

There is also a macro layer beneath that housing story. AP’s America In Focus package, published Friday, July 11, said Federal Reserve officials remain divided on where inflation is headed next. That matters because it keeps borrowers from assuming easy rate relief is right around the corner. If inflation still looks arguable from inside the Fed, then financing markets will keep pricing caution.

So the national setup this morning is fairly straightforward. The country is dealing with an extreme heat event, a new fight over press protections, deeper election-administration conflict and a housing market that is still too expensive for comfort. None of those stories shut down capital flows on their own. Together, they reinforce a backdrop where uncertainty keeps getting layered into everyday operating decisions.

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor, as always, is rates. I verified the latest official Treasury close available as of this Sunday run, which means Friday, July 10. The curve closed at 4.21 percent on the 2-year, 4.30 percent on the 5-year, 4.56 percent on the 10-year and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. That still looks like an open market, but not a forgiving one. The front end remains high enough that floating-rate debt cannot be treated casually. A 3.53 SOFR print sounds manageable only until lender spread, reserves, cap costs and extension risk are layered on top. The 5-year Treasury at 4.30 remains one of the most important numbers on the screen because it sits near the part of the curve where a lot of real executions are actually clearing. Borrowers who want certainty but do not want to pay full long-bond freight keep getting pulled into that middle lane. Then you get to the 30-year at 5.06, and that is where life-company money can still make sense, but mostly for clean stories that truly want duration and can live with disciplined leverage.

The broader Treasury shape matters too. Looking only at the 10-year misses too much of the real financing math. The 2-year tells you what floating debt still costs to carry. The 5-year tells you where practical fixed-rate negotiations are landing. The 30-year tells you why full-duration money is available but expensive. That is why the curve continues to argue for specificity rather than optimism. Borrowers are being rewarded for picking the right lane, not for hoping all lanes get cheaper.

The freshest large office financing datapoint remains the refinancing of 425 Lexington Avenue in Midtown Manhattan. JLL announced on Thursday, July 9, that it arranged a $352 million floating-rate SASB refinancing for Vanbarton Group through Goldman Sachs, with the loan pre-placed entirely with funds and accounts managed by BlackRock. That is a meaningful transaction because it says two things at once. First, institutional office liquidity still exists for the right tower, in the right location, with the right tenancy and sponsorship. Second, the execution path is highly curated. This is not evidence that generic office is suddenly easy. It is evidence that top-tier office can still clear when the capital-markets machinery is lined up properly from the start.

There is also a smaller but useful office CMBS signal from Washington. Commercial Observer published Friday, July 10, that Jemal Equities refinanced 1750 H Street NW with a $27 million CMBS loan from Citibank that Meridian Capital Group arranged. That matters because it shows conduit-style office execution is still alive beyond the trophy tier. The market will finance performing office when leasing momentum, debt yield and sponsorship line up. But it still wants proof. CMBS is available. It is just not generous.

That fits the broader securitized backdrop. Trepp reported on July 10 that the June CMBS delinquency rate improved by 20 basis points to 7.35 percent. That is directionally constructive, especially after a stretch where distress headlines were doing most of the talking. At the same time, Trepp’s recent spread work says five-year conduit loans have effectively become the market’s default setting, with median 2026 office spreads still running wider than multifamily and a touch wider than the overall conduit market. In other words, the market has breadth. What it does not have is much patience for ambiguity.

Dwight Mortgage Trust provided a $183 million construction loan for a 530-unit luxury multifamily development in Gilroy, California, which Connect described as the largest construction financing in Dwight’s history. Agency execution is still visible as well, even if the public tape is quieter than the debt-fund lane. The official agency signals support that read. If long-duration fixed rates stay expensive and borrowers keep prioritizing proceeds and certainty, HUD can come back into focus quickly. But as of this run, it is not the lane setting the tone.

The multifamily CMBS conversation also deserves a quick note. Apartment still prices materially better than office in conduit land, but it is not immune from refinancing friction. Loans originated under lower-rate assumptions still face proceeds pressure, and that means even good apartment collateral can require more borrower equity or more structuring discipline than sponsors expected a couple of years ago. Multifamily remains the best neighborhood in the market. It is just not a frictionless one.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The official Friday, July 10 Treasury close was 4.21 percent on the 2-year, 4.30 percent on the 5-year, 4.56 percent on the 10-year and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.53 percent for July 9. Freddie Mac’s average 30-year mortgage rate is 6.49 percent for the week ending July 9. Institutional office can still refinance when the asset quality is undeniable. CMBS remains open, but medium-duration structures are doing a lot of the work. Debt funds are still winning apartment construction assignments. Agency multifamily execution remains one of the cleanest permanent-debt lanes in the market.

One thing to watch this week is whether borrowers keep moving toward the middle of the curve instead of either floating indefinitely or paying up for maximum duration. If the 5-year Treasury stays materially inside the 30-year and SOFR remains sticky, five- to seven-year fixed-rate executions may keep looking like the market’s most rational compromise. If that continues, expect life companies to stay selective, banks to protect proceeds, CMBS to keep favoring disciplined structures and debt funds to remain the main solution set wherever the business plan is still dynamic.

The takeaway for this Sunday is simple. Nationally, the country is running hotter, more expensive and more litigious. In Debt Desk, capital is available, but it still charges for uncertainty. Trophy office can clear. Select office CMBS can clear. Multifamily remains the strongest financing story, especially when the collateral is clean or the development thesis is convincing. Agencies are open. Debt funds are important. And the rate curve is still telling borrowers to stop waiting for a perfect setup and start matching duration to what they can actually carry.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk Morning Brief for July 11, 2026
item.description: The national morning brief leads with a housing bill becoming law, an election administration shakeup, and a sharper AI copyright fight, before Debt Desk turns to a firmer Treasury curve, the latest SOFR print, fresh office and apartment financings, CMBS context, agency signals, and one thing to watch for July 11, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
It is Saturday, July 11th, and this is Debt Desk.

Let’s start with the national morning brief, because the clearest story this morning is that Washington, housing, and technology policy are all colliding with affordability and control at the same time.

The first headline is housing policy, and this one matters because it is moving from political theater into actual law. The Associated Press reported on Friday, July 10 that the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act will become law on Saturday, July 11 without President Donald Trump’s signature. The president said he was withholding his signature in protest over the Senate’s failure to advance a separate voter ID measure, but the housing bill still cleared Congress by wide margins and now goes live anyway. For the country, the immediate takeaway is not that affordability will suddenly improve overnight. It will not. The takeaway is that federal housing supply policy is finally moving again after years of gridlock. If implementation starts cleanly, that gives builders, lenders, and local governments a new framework to work with, even if the benefits arrive slowly.

That story connects directly to the second national headline, which is the broader question of who controls the rules of public life right now. AP also reported Friday that Trump ousted Democratic members of the bipartisan U.S. Election Assistance Commission, the agency that helps distribute federal election grants, oversees voting-system standards, and maintains the national voter registration form. On one level, this is a political power story. On another, it is an operating-environment story. When the machinery around elections becomes more contested, that affects public confidence, litigation risk, and the odds of more institutional friction heading into the midterms. Even for listeners focused mainly on markets, that matters. Capital does not just price cash flow. It prices political noise, implementation risk, and the chance that operational systems get pulled into legal fights.

The third headline keeps the focus on control, but in a very different arena. AP reported that major news organizations asked a federal judge in Manhattan to sanction OpenAI in the copyright case over whether AI models were trained on news content without permission. The filing centers on alleged discovery misconduct, but the bigger story is that this fight is becoming more concrete. It is no longer just a philosophical debate over whether AI changes media economics. It is now a legal battle over evidence, records, and leverage. That matters for publishers, of course, but it also matters for the broader business landscape because it touches how intellectual property is valued, how licensing negotiations may evolve, and how much legal uncertainty companies will have to carry while the AI buildout continues.

The fourth headline is housing again, but this time through the lens of household affordability rather than legislation. AP reported Friday that existing-home sales in June fell to a 4.09 million annual pace while the median home price hit a record $440,600. Freddie Mac separately said the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 6.49 percent in the week ending July 9. That combination is the uncomfortable truth of the American housing market right now. Activity is soft, borrowing costs are still elevated, and yet prices remain high enough to keep affordability tight. When sales can slow without producing real price relief, it tells you supply is still constrained and households are still being forced into hard tradeoffs. It also tells you why apartment demand, renter retention, and multifamily lender attention remain so important to this audience.

Put those stories together and the national setup this morning is pretty clean. Washington is still making major decisions through conflict rather than calm consensus. Housing remains both a policy priority and a household strain. The legal architecture around artificial intelligence is still being written in real time. And for markets, none of that is abstract. It all feeds into confidence, capital allocation, and the price of patience.

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor, as always, is rates, and today’s official figures moved higher from the prior session. I verified the Friday, July 10 Treasury close using the project’s market-data checker against the official Treasury table. The 2-year closed at 4.21 percent, the 5-year at 4.30 percent, the 10-year at 4.56 percent, and the 30-year at 5.06 percent. I also verified through the New York Fed API that the latest official SOFR print is 3.53 percent for Thursday, July 9.

That rate picture matters because it says the financing market is still open, but it is not getting easier by accident. The front end is high enough that floating-rate debt still has to be earned. SOFR at 3.53 is manageable for the right bridge loan, but it is not low enough to make carry feel casual, especially once you layer in lender spread, reserves, and the cost of a cap. The 5-year Treasury at 4.30 is arguably the most important number on the screen for actual borrower behavior because it sits in the part of the curve where many real-world execution conversations now clear. It offers materially less duration cost than the long bond while still giving borrowers a real hedge against rate volatility. Then you get to the 30-year at 5.06, and that is where life-company money can still show up, but mostly for borrowers who truly want long-duration certainty and can live with more disciplined leverage.

The shape of the curve also reinforces something borrowers have been learning repeatedly this year. The 10-year is still a useful benchmark, but it is no longer enough on its own. If you ignore the 2-year, you miss the carry burden on floating debt. If you ignore the 5-year, you miss where a lot of practical permanent debt is being priced. If you ignore the 30-year, you miss why some borrowers like the idea of duration more than they like the actual coupon that comes with it.

Against that backdrop, the most useful question is not whether money exists. It does. The real question is what kind of collateral and what kind of story can actually command good execution.

The freshest large office datapoint is still the July 9 refinancing of 425 Lexington Avenue in Midtown Manhattan. Connect CRE reported that Vanbarton Group secured a $352 million floating-rate SASB refinancing through Goldman Sachs, and the loan was fully pre-placed with BlackRock-managed funds and accounts. That is a big deal for two reasons. First, it confirms that large institutional office paper can still attract real liquidity when the asset, location, and sponsorship are strong enough. Second, it shows what the current capital stack often looks like when office does clear. This is not broad-based easy bank balance-sheet lending. It is highly curated, capital-markets-heavy execution with institutional buyers already lined up.

There was also a fresh CMBS office datapoint on Friday that matters because it lands lower on the quality spectrum than a Midtown trophy office story. Commercial Observer reported July 10 that Jemal Equities refinanced 1750 H Street NW in Washington, D.C., with a $27 million CMBS loan. The amount is obviously much smaller than the Lexington Avenue refinancing, but the signal still matters. CMBS remains a live execution lane for performing office, not just for apartments, industrial, or the cleanest suburban assets. The catch is that office still pays for scrutiny. The market will finance it, but it wants clarity on tenancy, rollover, debt yield, and sponsorship before it commits.

That is where the broader CMBS backdrop helps explain the tone. Trepp reported on July 6 that the June CMBS delinquency rate fell 20 basis points to 7.35 percent, helped by a large lodging cure. That is directionally constructive. At the same time, Trepp’s July hard-maturities work says 36 percent of 2026 hard maturities are sitting at debt yields of 8 percent or below, which is exactly the band where refinance friction becomes hard to ignore. In other words, delinquency optics improved, but that does not mean refinance math suddenly got forgiving. CMBS is functioning. It is just functioning with discipline.

Trepp’s recent conduit spread work also supports the idea that five-year CMBS has become the market’s practical default in many situations. Median five-year conduit spreads have stabilized in the high-200-basis-point range, while office continues to price wider than multifamily and industrial. That lines up with what the broader deal tape suggests. Borrowers are willing to meet the market in medium-duration fixed-rate structures when it buys certainty at a tolerable cost. They are less eager to pay all the way up for very long paper unless the asset and hold strategy really justify it.

So the lender tone this morning looks like this. Banks are still participating, but selectively and often where sponsorship, deposits, or relationship value support the file. Life companies are open for clean, stabilized product, especially multifamily, but the long end of the Treasury curve keeps them disciplined. CMBS is competitive where debt yield and story quality line up. Debt funds remain the flexibility provider when the assignment involves construction, repositioning, lease-up, or an asset type that conventional lenders still underwrite defensively.

That is the perfect bridge into multifamily, because apartments continue to provide the deepest and most consistent financing tape in the market.

The freshest headline there came Friday from Connect CRE, which reported that Dwight Mortgage Trust provided a $183 million construction loan for a 530-unit luxury multifamily development in Gilroy, California. Connect noted that it is the largest construction financing in Dwight’s history. That is a meaningful signal. Even with construction lending still selective, debt funds are clearly willing to step up for apartment projects when scale, sponsorship, and submarket logic line up. In other words, multifamily is still the place where private credit is most willing to take development risk when the exit story is believable.

Agency financing remains active as well, especially for straightforward permanent debt. Connect CRE reported on July 9 that Northmarq arranged $22.855 million in Fannie Mae DUS acquisition financing for Elora Flats and Townhomes in Lawrence, Massachusetts. The structure carried a seven-year term with four years of interest-only. That is exactly the kind of deal that reminds you why agencies still matter so much in this market. When the asset is stable, the affordability profile is attractive, and the borrower wants durable execution rather than maximal leverage, agency debt still offers one of the cleanest permanent financing lanes available.

The public agency signals also remain constructive even without a splashy July 10 or July 11 closing announcement from Washington. Freddie Mac Multifamily published an insurance-related update on July 7 and continues to show active conventional lending lanes through its platform. Fannie Mae’s Guide Update 26-16 on insurance became effective on July 6, which is another quiet but real sign that the agency machine is current and moving. HUD and FHA are still quieter in the near-term headline flow. The HUD multifamily mortgagee-letter page still points mainly to earlier 2026 actions, including changes tied to the MAP Guide and middle-income housing, rather than a new July apartment execution that would reset the conversation this week.

That does not mean HUD is irrelevant. It means HUD is not the loudest signal in the market right now. The louder signal is that private credit and agencies are doing more of the visible work, while banks remain more selective and CMBS continues to help where the asset profile can support securitized execution.

The multifamily CMBS angle is worth one more quick note. Apartments still look healthier than most major property types, but they are not exempt from maturity stress. The same Trepp hard-maturity framework that flags office and retail also catches a meaningful slice of multifamily loans that were originated under very different rate assumptions. So apartment debt is still the best neighborhood on the block, just not a frictionless one.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The official July 10 Treasury close was 4.21 percent on the 2-year, 4.30 percent on the 5-year, 4.56 percent on the 10-year, and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.53 percent for July 9. Freddie Mac’s average 30-year mortgage rate is 6.49 percent for the week ending July 9. Office financing is available for top-tier assets and for select CMBS-ready properties, but execution still rewards clarity. Multifamily continues to draw the broadest lender interest across agencies and debt funds. And the curve still argues for careful duration decisions rather than reflexively reaching for either pure floating debt or the longest fixed-rate money on the shelf.

One thing to watch over the next few sessions is whether medium-duration fixed-rate executions keep separating from both floating-rate bridge loans and full-duration long-bond money. If the 5-year Treasury stays meaningfully inside the 30-year and SOFR holds where it is, that middle lane may remain the market’s most practical clearing point. If that happens, expect more borrowers to choose five- to seven-year certainty, expect life companies to stay selective, and expect debt funds to keep winning the assignments where the business plan is still too dynamic for conventional lenders.

The takeaway for this Saturday is straightforward. Nationally, the country is still trying to solve affordability, institutional control, and AI-era legal risk all at once. In Debt Desk, money is available, but it still prices ambiguity aggressively. Trophy office can clear. Select CMBS office can clear. Multifamily remains the strongest financing story. Agencies are still active. Debt funds still matter most where complexity begins. And the rate curve is still telling borrowers to think less about what sounds optimal in theory and more about what they can actually carry in practice.

It is Friday, July 10th, and this is Debt Desk.

Let’s start with the national morning brief, because today the country is waking up to a familiar but still uncomfortable combination: a labor market that is holding together without much momentum, a housing market that keeps getting more expensive even when volumes soften, and a technology fight that is starting to look less theoretical and more operational.

The first story this morning is the labor market, and the signal is steady but not especially strong. The Associated Press reported Thursday that first-time jobless claims fell by 2,000 to 215,000 for the week ended July 4. That is still a healthy level by historical standards, and it tells you layoffs are not accelerating in a way that would immediately change the macro conversation. But that is only half the picture. The same AP coverage noted that June hiring slowed materially, which means employers are still cautious even if they are not cutting deeply. For markets, that keeps the economy in an awkward middle ground. It is not weak enough to force quick policy relief, but it is not strong enough to erase concerns about slower growth.

The second story is housing affordability, and there are really two fresh headlines that belong together. AP reported Thursday that existing-home sales in June fell 2.4 percent from May to a 4.09 million annual pace, while the median sales price climbed 1.8 percent from a year earlier to a record $440,600. AP separately reported that the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose this week to 6.49 percent from 6.43 percent. Put those together and the story is straightforward: supply is still not loose enough to bring prices down meaningfully, financing costs have moved back up, and the result is a market where activity can soften without real affordability relief. That matters well beyond single-family housing. It shapes renter demand, keeps apartment fundamentals supported in many markets, and reinforces why multifamily remains the cleanest story in the broader property lending universe.

The third national story is the legal fight over artificial intelligence and copyrighted content. AP reported Thursday that several major news organizations, including The New York Times and the Daily News, asked a federal judge in New York to sanction OpenAI in the ongoing copyright case over how AI models were trained on news content. The immediate issue is discovery conduct, but the broader implication is bigger than courtroom procedure. This is becoming a fight over what inputs AI companies are allowed to use, how those inputs are documented, and how much economic leverage publishers can recover. For investors, lenders, and business operators, the practical takeaway is that the AI buildout remains a growth story, but the legal architecture around content, data rights, and commercial usage is still very much under construction.

The fourth story is less about markets directly and more about the broader public backdrop. AP reported Thursday that eight men were indicted over an alleged plot to attack the White House event known as Freedom 250 using drones and sniper fire. Authorities say the plan was disrupted before the event, but the story still matters because it is another reminder that domestic security risk is not abstract. It affects event planning, insurance, policing, and public confidence. Even when a story like this does not move markets on its own, it contributes to the sense that the operating environment across politics, public gatherings, and civic institutions remains tense.

So the national setup this morning is clear enough. The labor market is stable, but softer underneath the surface. Housing remains expensive even as sales cool. The AI legal fight is escalating. And the wider public atmosphere is still carrying a lot of tension. None of that closes markets. All of it shapes how capital prices risk.

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor, as always, is rates. I verified the latest official Treasury close through the project checker for Thursday, July 9. The curve closed at 4.16 percent on the 2-year, 4.27 percent on the 5-year, 4.54 percent on the 10-year, and 5.05 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.58 percent for July 8.

That curve is saying several things at once. The front end is no longer screaming emergency, but it is still high enough that floating-rate debt remains a real carrying-cost question. The 5-year at 4.27 matters because that part of the curve is increasingly where practical borrower conversations live. It offers more certainty than floating debt without forcing every borrower to pay all the way out the curve for full-duration money. The 10-year at 4.54 still works for permanent debt, but it does not make proceeds magically easy. And the 30-year above 5 percent continues to matter because it keeps long-duration fixed-rate execution available, yet selective. When the long bond is that elevated, life companies can still be attractive for the cleanest assets, but only for borrowers who truly want duration and can live with lower leverage and tighter structures.

SOFR at 3.58 is better than the worst prints borrowers had to absorb earlier in the cycle, but it is not low enough to make bridge debt feel casual. Floating-rate structures are workable when the business plan is short, the cap is in place, and the takeout story is believable. They become much less forgiving when sponsors are still depending on future rate relief to solve today’s underwriting gap.

The next question is what kinds of deals are actually getting done. The freshest office datapoint is Connect CRE’s July 9 report that Vanbarton Group refinanced 425 Lexington Avenue in Manhattan with a $352 million floating-rate single-asset, single-borrower loan through Goldman Sachs that was fully pre-placed with BlackRock-managed funds and accounts. That is a useful signal because it shows large, institutional office can still access serious capital when the asset quality, location, and sponsorship are strong enough. It also shows how execution is being assembled right now. This is not generic easy-money bank lending. It is structured, placement-driven capital going to a trophy-caliber story that can survive close scrutiny.

You can see a similar tone in transitional or more specialized property types. Commercial Observer reported July 7 that Keyah Real Estate Group landed $38 million from Maxim Credit Group to reposition a Miami Beach hotel into a Treehouse-branded property. That is not plain-vanilla stabilized hospitality debt. It is business-plan capital, and the lender is a private-credit style source comfortable with repositioning risk. The lesson is the same one the market has been teaching for months: when the story gets more complex, the debt-fund lane gets more important.

Life-company capital is still there too, but it is acting exactly the way you would expect with the 30-year Treasury above 5 percent. Commercial Observer reported Thursday that Pacific Life Insurance provided a $125 million refinancing for the Arthur on Aberdeen, a 363-unit luxury apartment tower in Chicago that opened in 2024. That is a clean illustration of current life-company behavior. Stabilized or near-stabilized multifamily, strong sponsorship, durable cash flow, and a borrower willing to prioritize certainty over maximum leverage can still find very good long-term money. But the long end of the curve is not letting that money get sloppy.

The CMBS conversation remains constructive, but careful. Trepp reported last week that the June CMBS delinquency rate fell 20 basis points to 7.35 percent, helped by a large lodging cure. That is directionally positive. At the same time, Trepp’s July hard-maturities analysis says refinance friction remains real, especially where older office and retail loans still face a gap between in-place cash flow and today’s execution standards. Trepp’s recent conduit spread work also points to a market that increasingly favors five-year structures over automatically defaulting to ten-year conduit debt. That lines up with what borrowers are seeing in practice. CMBS is open. It is just not open in a carefree way.

So the spread and execution tone this morning looks like this. Banks and capital-markets desks are still showing up for strong sponsorship and high-quality collateral, especially when the asset can attract institutional placement. Life companies remain selective because the long bond is expensive and duration has to be earned. CMBS is functioning, but borrowers still need debt yield, stability, and a story that can hold together under securitized underwriting. Debt funds remain the flexibility provider, especially when the assignment includes construction, repositioning, lease-up, or some other element conventional lenders would rather avoid.

Now let’s move into multifamily, where the tape continues to offer the clearest read on where lenders still have conviction.

One of the freshest debt-fund signals came from Commercial Observer on Thursday, which reported that S3 Capital provided $28 million for a new multifamily construction project in Texas. The headline amount is not giant, but the message is important. Construction capital for apartments is still available when the deal size is right, the local supply picture is understandable, and the sponsor has a coherent path from build to stabilization. This is exactly the sort of slot where debt funds keep winning business.

South Florida also produced a fresh private-credit style datapoint. Commercial Observer’s Thursday finance coverage highlighted a new $54 million residential loan for Dependable Equities in Fort Lauderdale. Even without pretending that every South Florida apartment deal is interchangeable, the tape keeps saying the same thing: lenders are still active there, but they want clarity on submarket demand, exit strategy, and sponsor execution.

The bank-and-agency side of the apartment market is active too. Connect CRE reported on July 9 that Northmarq arranged $22.855 million in acquisition financing for the 104-unit Elora Flats and Townhomes in Lawrence, Massachusetts, through its in-house Fannie Mae DUS platform. The structure included a seven-year term with four years of interest-only payments. That matters because it is a clean real-world reminder that agency lending is still doing exactly what it is supposed to do: financing straightforward multifamily with durable cash flow through an efficient permanent-debt channel.

Freddie Mac’s public issuance calendar also remains worth watching. The latest calendar, dated July 1, shows conventional fixed-rate, floating-rate, tax-exempt, and CRT-related activity still moving through the pipeline. The current participation-certificate calendar is especially helpful because it shows live loan examples with current coupons and spreads, including floating-rate apartment paper priced off SOFR. That does not mean every borrower can get Freddie execution on command. It does mean the agency machine is active, current, and still a meaningful outlet for stabilized multifamily debt.

Fannie Mae is sending a quieter but still relevant signal. Its Multifamily Guide page shows Guide Update 26-16 on insurance became effective July 6, following other early-July guidance updates. That is not a splashy headline, but it tells you the agency channel is not dormant. The rules are current, underwriting remains active, and lenders originating into that system are still operating in a functioning permanent market.

HUD and FHA are quieter this morning. I did not find a fresh multifamily execution or policy development from HUD in the last 24 hours that deserved to lead this section. The public HUD multifamily memos and letters pages still point back to older 2026 items rather than a new July headline. In practical terms, that means HUD remains available as a lane, but not the lane setting the tone in this week’s public market conversation. Right now the louder signals are still coming from agencies, banks, and private credit.

The multifamily CMBS backdrop also deserves a quick note. Apartment remains the healthiest mainstream property type in the lending market, but that does not exempt it from refinance math. Trepp’s latest work still shows that maturing loans originated under very different rate assumptions can run into lower proceeds even when property fundamentals are better than office or retail. So the apartment story remains the best one in the room, just not a frictionless one.

The concise markets snapshot this morning is this. The latest verified Treasury curve is 4.16 percent on the 2-year, 4.27 percent on the 5-year, 4.54 percent on the 10-year, and 5.05 percent on the 30-year as of the July 9 close. The latest official SOFR print is 3.58 percent for July 8. The average 30-year mortgage rate is back up to 6.49 percent. The labor market still looks stable, but not vibrant. Institutional-quality office can still clear large refinancings. Debt funds remain important for construction and repositioning. Agencies are still active in multifamily. CMBS sentiment is somewhat better than it was a month ago, but maturities still argue for caution.

One thing to watch today is whether borrowers keep clustering around medium-duration fixed-rate structures instead of paying for maximum duration. With the 5-year Treasury meaningfully inside the 30-year and SOFR still high enough to make bridge debt expensive, that middle zone of the curve looks increasingly like the market’s practical clearing point. If that continues, expect more executions that favor five- to seven-year certainty, more selective life-company bidding, and continued demand for debt funds whenever the business plan gets too complicated for conventional balance-sheet lenders.

The takeaway for this Friday is simple. Nationally, the economy still looks resilient, but expensive and legally messy. In Debt Desk, the market is open, but it is charging for ambiguity. Clean multifamily still has the deepest lender bench. Trophy office can still get done with the right structure. Debt funds are still solving the complicated assignments. And the curve is still telling borrowers to be honest about what kind of certainty they really need to buy.

It is Thursday, July 9th, and this is Debt Desk.

Let’s start with the national morning brief, because this morning the macro tone is coming from policy uncertainty, construction risk, and political instability all at once, and each of those themes feeds back into capital markets faster than people like to admit.

The biggest national headline for markets is the Federal Reserve. The Associated Press reported Wednesday that the minutes from the Fed’s June meeting showed a real split inside the committee over whether inflation stays stubborn or cools off once war-related energy pressure fades. That matters because this is not a market debating whether the Fed is comfortable. It is a market debating whether policy is restrictive enough. If half the committee can still see rates going higher by year-end while the other half sees a hold or even some easing, borrowers should assume the path forward is still noisy. For lenders, that usually means discipline stays in place. For borrowers, it means any financing strategy built around imminent rate relief is still more hope than plan.

The second national story is the Manhattan conversion scare near Grand Central, and this one lands unusually close to the Debt Desk audience. AP reported Wednesday that the damaged former Pfizer headquarters was stabilized after buckled columns and sagging floors forced evacuations, but the city is now moving into a broader investigation of what went wrong. That is important because this is not just a local construction story. It is a live reminder that adaptive reuse remains compelling in theory but unforgiving in execution. Office-to-residential conversions still attract policy support and investor interest, yet the market is being reminded in real time that complexity can show up late, expensively, and publicly. That affects schedules, insurance conversations, contingency reserves, and ultimately lender confidence.

The third story is Washington uncertainty around Mitch McConnell. AP reported Wednesday that Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear publicly asked McConnell to provide a health update after weeks of silence following his June 14 hospitalization. Senate leaders have said they have spoken with him and that he is engaged, but the issue is now plainly political as well as personal. The reason markets care is not that McConnell alone changes the economic outlook. It is that leadership uncertainty can complicate Senate timing, vote management, and expectations around how cleanly Washington can move through the next set of fiscal and policy fights. In a market already sensitive to deficits, tariffs, and inflation, that kind of uncertainty tends to keep risk premiums sticky.

The fourth story is healthcare policy, where AP reported that Planned Parenthood and two smaller regional providers are resuming Medicaid billing for non-abortion services after almost a year of cutoff. The billing resumed on Sunday, but the update is still developing because the operating damage outlasted the formal funding gap. Clinics have closed, staffing has been lost, and some services are not expected to come back even after reimbursement restarted. For investors and lenders, the lesson is broader than the politics. Funding volatility can leave lasting scars on local service ecosystems, and those second-order effects matter for communities, labor markets, and municipal stability well after the headline appears settled.

So the national setup this morning is straightforward. The Fed is still split. A marquee Manhattan conversion is stable but under scrutiny. Senate uncertainty is still alive. And even when policy swings reverse, local operating disruption can linger.

Now let’s turn to Debt Desk.

The first anchor is rates, and as of this early Thursday run the latest official Treasury close available is Wednesday, July 8. Verified through the project’s market-data checker, the curve closed at 4.21 percent on the 2-year, 4.31 percent on the 5-year, 4.56 percent on the 10-year, and 5.06 percent on the 30-year. The latest official SOFR print is 3.62 percent for July 7.

That is not a broken market, but it is still a demanding one. The front end remains high enough that floating-rate borrowers do not get to relax. The 5-year matters because it sits close to where a lot of practical fixed-rate negotiations actually happen for borrowers who want some certainty without paying all the way up for maximum duration. The 10-year at 4.56 is not catastrophic, but it still requires discipline on proceeds and debt service coverage. And the 30-year back above 5 percent keeps long-duration fixed-rate money useful, not generous.

The shape of that curve is doing real work right now. The gap between the 5-year and the 30-year is still wide enough that plenty of borrowers are going to ask whether full-duration execution is worth the extra cost. That is especially relevant for life companies. Their capital is still very real, and for the cleanest low-leverage stories it remains one of the most attractive forms of permanent debt in the market.
